Hi Alex —

Thanks again for the call today — really appreciate you walking through FastPay's latency/throughput expectations and the production constraints. Quick recap and a proposed next step so we can align the SLO language and autoscale behavior for the POC: 

Key takeaways from today
- Target p95 latency: 150ms for single-turn text generation (streaming enabled).
- Typical traffic: steady-state ~500 req/s across US region; planned peak bursts up to ~1000 req/s during promos.
- Concurrency: endpoints see ~200 concurrent open streams on average; spikes push concurrent streams to ~600 for short periods.
- Streaming: you rely on chunked streaming to render tokens as they arrive; tail latency on the first token is critical for UX.
- Availability/queueing: acceptable to queue short bursts (up to 30s) before scale completes, but queued requests must not push p95 above target.

Autoscale & warm pool notes (from our brief):
- Warm pool concept: maintain a pool of pre-warmed workers (with model loaded and KV cache warmed) to handle rapid scale-up for bursts.
- Desired scale-up SLA: prefer <90s to handle 80% of burst events; acceptable up to 3 minutes for fully cold scale.
- Pricing/commits: you'll want a small reserved warm pool during promos to avoid excessive tail latency.

Attachments: I attached a short SLO/price sketch and an autoscale diagram for your review (redwood-slo-proposal.pdf, autoscale-diagram.png).

Proposed next steps
1) Dev deep-dive with our SE to validate warm-pool sizing and streaming behavior (can we do Mon 8 Mar or Tue 9 Mar?).
2) I'll circulate a short SLO proposal (attached) that maps p95/p99 language to throughput & warm-pool commitments.
3) If that looks good, we can prepare a limited POC for the promo window you mentioned.

Can you confirm availability for the SE session and whether we should loop in your procurement contact (contracts@fastpay.com) now or after SLO alignment?

Hi Alex — thanks for the questions, happy to dig in. Below are concrete details we usually share for a POC and what to expect operationally.

Warm pool & scale behavior (short summary)
- Warm pool: we keep a configurable number of worker processes (model and libs loaded, KV cache seeded if you choose) in a ready state. These are the fastest path for handling bursts — they can accept requests within ~20–40s for streaming-heavy workloads (initial token latency optimized).
- Near-warm nodes: need partial model load or layer init; typically come up in ~45–90s depending on model size and GPU type.
- Cold scale (new GPU instance + model): worst-case ~2–5 minutes depending on cloud instance startup and model weights.

Queueing & prioritization
- By default we use a short FIFO queue per route and backpressure signals to the gateway. We can prioritize in-flight/streaming sessions over new non-stream requests if you want — this reduces visible stalls for open streams.
- Queue time target: we can configure a soft queue cutoff (e.g., 30s) after which requests fail fast or are redirected to a lower-cost fallback model.

Sizing rules of thumb
- For streaming endpoints, size warm pool by concurrent streams (aim for 10–20% of expected peak concurrency as a starting point).
- For non-streaming batch endpoints, size by throughput (req/s) and average tokens — a small warm pool covering ~5–10% of peak req/s often dramatically improves tail latency.

Operational knobs we recommend during POC
- Reserve a small warm pool for promo windows (static allocation) + dynamic warm-up policy based on rolling averages.
- Enable KV prefix caching for hot users to reduce per-request decode time.
- Use gradual ramp-up policy: allow short queueing and then scale additional nodes if queue length crosses threshold.

Attached high-level diagram shows warm pool vs cold provisioning timelines (autoscale-diagram.png). I'm happy to demo these behaviors in our SE session — we can run a short synthetic spike to show p95 impact with/without warm pool.
